To interlard something means to insert or scatter extra elements throughout a piece of writing, speech, or conversation — mixing them in at various points, not just at the beginning or end.

Think of it like raisins in a bread loaf. The raisins don't replace the bread — they're dotted throughout it, interrupting the plain dough again and again. That's what interlarding does: it takes something and drops additions into it, repeatedly, at different points.
The Most Important Thing to Know: Its Connotation

This is where the word gets interesting and where learners often miss the full picture.

Interlard almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone. When someone says a speech or a piece of writing is "interlarded" with something, they are usually suggesting that those inserted elements are:

  • Excessive — there are too many of them
  • Out of place — they don't quite belong
  • Disrupting — they break the natural flow of what's being said

It's not a neutral word like include or contain. It implies the additions feel somewhat crammed in or awkwardly stuffed into something that would have been fine — or even better — without them.

The word is used almost exclusively in the context of language — spoken or written. Common things that get interlarded include:

  • Technical jargon in a speech meant for a general audience
  • Jokes or anecdotes in an otherwise serious essay
  • Foreign words or phrases dropped into everyday conversation
  • Quotations, digressions, or footnotes scattered throughout a text
  • Flattery or irrelevant remarks mixed into a formal letter

The most common structure is:

[Something] is interlarded with [the inserted elements]

Or:

[Someone] interlards [something] with [the inserted elements]

Example 1:

"His lecture was interlarded with so many Latin phrases that the students lost the thread completely."

→ He kept dropping Latin phrases throughout his lecture, and it made things harder to follow.

Example 2:

"She interlarded her business proposal with personal stories that had nothing to do with the project."

→ She scattered unrelated personal stories throughout the proposal. The implication is that this weakened it.

Example 3:

"The article was interlarded with technical footnotes, making it exhausting to read."

→ Footnotes kept interrupting the reading experience throughout the article.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words seem close to interlard, but each has a distinct feel:

  • Sprinkle with — gentle and usually positive ("sprinkled with wit"). No negative weight.
  • Pepper with — more energetic and frequent ("peppered with questions"), but still fairly neutral or lively in tone.
  • Intersperse with — purely descriptive and neutral ("interspersed with photographs"). No judgment at all.
  • Pad with — suggests adding bulk to fill space, often unnecessary filler.
  • Interlard with — implies the additions feel intrusive or overdone, disrupting what they're inserted into. This is the most critical of the group.

The key distinction of interlard is that it judges. It quietly tells the reader: these insertions didn't improve things.
The Register of the Word Itself

Interlard is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. It appears most commonly in:

  • Literary criticism and book reviews
  • Essays and academic writing
  • Journalism, particularly cultural or political commentary

Using it signals that the speaker or writer is educated and precise in their language.
The Complete Picture in One Sentence

To interlard something is to repeatedly insert additional material throughout a piece of speech or writing, and the word quietly signals that these insertions are excessive, ill-fitting, or disruptive to the overall flow.
